newsitem.title: THAILAND: Analysts urge austerity after Thai ratings shock.
newsitem.headline: Analysts urge austerity after Thai ratings shock.

text.p: Thailand, jolted by a downgrade of its short-term sovereign debt ratings by Moody's Investors Service, should adopt austere economic policies to bolster creditor confidence, financial analysts said on Thursday.

The move to downgrade the ratings for Thai bank deposits and other obligations would raise foreign borrowing costs for private Thai borrowers by 25-50 basis points and delay domestic lending rate cuts expected later this year, they said.
Moody's on Tuesday also downgraded short-term deposit ratings of Bangkok Bank Plc, Siam Commercial Bank Plc and Thai Farmers Bank Plc to Prime 2 from Prime 1.

"It is a reminder that Thailand should focus on curbing its current account deficit and inflation to convince foreign creditors it would have no problem financing short-term borrowing," said Charl Kengchon of Thai Farmers Research. "This is a time to pursue monetary disciplines," he said.
Finance Minister Bodi Chunnananda said on Thursday that Thailand may take additional restrictive measures if necessary to maintain its current "A-2" long-term credit ratings given by Moody's.
He pledged that the government would continue its policy of the past eight years of maintaining a national balanced budget.
The Moody's announcement capped a string of negative news for Thailand since July, when its weak export figures prompted the Bank of Thailand to scale down economic growth projections.
Thai exports rose 3.8 percent during the January-July period against a 26.2 percent increase the same period a year ago.

The central bank's mid-year adjustment of key indicators, including a forecast for a wider current account deficit and lower 1996 gross domestic product growth, prompted currency dealers to put sporadic pressure on the baht in late July and early August.

The Bank of Thailand moderated its 1996 GDP growth forecast to 7.8 percent from 8.1, and raised its current account deficit estimate to 7.8 percent of GDP from 6.5. But private economists still viewed the revised projections as optimistic and doubted if they could be achieved.

The Bank of Thailand said about 47.5 percent of foreign loans to the private sector in July was short-term debt. But it added that 61 percent of the short-term borrowing was made through offshore banking units that was normally extended or rolled over several times on maturity.

Thanawat Pachimkul of Seamico Securities Plc said the central bank had tried since late 1995 to slow short-term capital inflow by raising cash reserve requirements for financial firms when they import funds for relending.

He said Thailand would need time to boost exports and trim its current account deficit but inflation was expected to be sharply lower in the next few months after averaging 6.6 percent in the first eight months of this year.
But Charl said an expected Thai minimum wage hike in October and rising oil prices may prevent Thailand from meeting its revised 5.5 percent inflation target this year.
